analysis.investment_thesis: Aadhar Housing Finance is a financial company — the Magic Formula explicitly excludes this category because debt is an operating input, not leverage, making EBIT/EV and ROIC meaningless. While the business shows a strong 33.4% net profit CAGR and 16.1% revenue CAGR, I cannot rank it against non-financial companies on my core metrics.
key_strengths: Net Profit CAGR of 33.4% over 6 years (INR 162 Cr → 912 Cr) demonstrates real earnings compounding
Revenue expanding at 16.1% CAGR; operating income CAGR of 21.3% (FY22–25) shows operating leverage
Equity base grew from INR 2,347 Cr (2020) to INR 6,894 Cr (2025); strong capital position post-IPO
key_risks: ROE of 16.9% and ROCE of 11.4% are mediocre — not the kind of high-return business the Magic Formula targets
Debt/Equity of 2.55x is moderate for an HFC but borrowing costs (INR 1,174 Cr in FY25) are rising faster than revenue
P/B of 3.11x is elevated for a business with sub-17% ROE — implies premium that needs sustained growth to justify
red_flags: Operating CF persistently negative (0/5 years positive) — standard for lending but impossible to analyze via FCF yield
Magic Formula explicitly excludes financial companies: EBIT/EV and ROIC calculations are structurally inapplicable
Finance costs (INR 1,174 Cr FY25) now represent 38% of revenue — spread compression risk if rates rise
analysis.detailed_analysis:
The Magic Formula cannot be applied here. Aadhar Housing Finance is a mortgage lender: its liabilities (INR 16,322 Cr debt) fund assets (loans), and 'negative OCF' simply means loan disbursements exceed collections — normal for a growing HFC. Earnings yield computed on EBIT/EV and ROIC on net working capital would produce nonsensical results because the capital structure IS the business model. I penalize this stock not because the business is bad, but because my methodology offers no insight.

On the qualitative side, AADHARHFC serves affordable housing in underbanked geographies with a government-backed tailwind. Net profit growth of 33% CAGR is real and sustained over 6 years. But at P/E 20.8x and P/B 3.11x with ROE only 16.9%, it is not a cheap business earning high returns on capital — the two criteria I require. A specialist financials analyst would evaluate NIM, credit quality, and AUM growth; that is not my framework.
